answer:
I ran the experiment as 4 circuits in one job on emerald:mock. Each circuit used all 54 qubits and 250 shots. Nothing went to a real QPU, so no credits were spent.

How I built it. The real emerald calibration set (3a1a9ad0-0c98-49db-8cf5-7623d13729f4) lists 83 working CZ couplers. The mock lists 90, but I used the 83 from the real machine as you asked. Each time step puts RX(theta) on every qubit and then one gate on each of the 83 couplers. Each coupler gate exp(i pi/4 ZZ) is exactly one CZ plus a Z rotation of -pi/2 on each of its two qubits. I folded those Z rotations into the phase of the next RX pulse. That way each coupler gate is one CZ and nothing else. I sent the circuits as IQM native instructions (prx, cz, measure), so no compiler pass ran on them. I read the circuits back from the server afterwards. All 4 matched what I sent, gate for gate. Each one has 249 CZ gates (83 couplers times 3 steps), each step uses every coupler once, and each measures QB1 to QB54. I checked on small patches of the lattice that the CZ version and the original RX plus RZZ version give the same physics. The first mock job (01a16489-1b4e-73bb-8b90-6b876895d3f6) was the test. The second (01a16489-4ed2-7367-bea6-1cb3d722941c) is the stand-in for real emerald. The API reported 1.0 billed second for it, but mock jobs cost 0 credits.

What a perfect quantum computer gives (magnetization, the average of Z):
- theta = 0: 1.000. A zero-strength field leaves every spin pointing up.
- theta = 0.2 pi: 0.446
- theta = 0.35 pi: 0.102
- theta = 0.5 pi: 0.000

This is the melting you wanted to see. A stronger sideways field tips the spins over, and the coupler gates spread that disorder to the neighbors. After 3 steps the sheet has lost most or all of its magnetization.

What the mock returned: -0.013, -0.006, 0.013, 0.013. These numbers are all close to 0, and the theta = 0 circuit also gives close to 0 instead of 1. The reason is that the mock does not run the circuit. It returns made-up bitstrings that have nothing to do with the gates. So the noise-corrected values are meaningless here. Dividing by the theta = 0 result, which is -0.013, gives 0.50, -1.06, and -1.02. Real numbers would sit between 0 and 1, so these values are not physical. On real emerald, noise would shrink the theta = 0 value below 1. Dividing by it would then undo part of that shrinking, and the corrected values could come close to 0.45, 0.10, and 0.

Could a laptop compute this? Yes. I computed the perfect-machine values above on a laptop in seconds. After 3 steps, each spin is affected only by spins within 2 couplers of it. That is at most 13 qubits, and a laptop can simulate 13 qubits exactly. Also, at theta = 0.5 pi every gate is a Clifford gate, and computers can simulate Clifford circuits quickly even at large sizes. So this is not a quantum advantage. To have a chance at one, you would need many more steps, so that each spin's region of influence grows too large for classical methods. You would also need results good enough to trust, and today's noise makes that hard.
